name: Hormone bloodwork panel (total/free T, SHBG, E2, LH)

lead: A hormone panel measures total testosterone, often free testosterone and SHBG, estradiol and LH. Looksmaxxers order it as a first step to see where their hormones stand before working on muscle, leanness and skin.

Clinicians use these tests to diagnose low testosterone and tell primary from secondary hypogonadism: LH is high in primary and low or normal in secondary. Guidelines cited by Wikipedia say a total testosterone below 300 ng/dL can support a diagnosis, and free or bioavailable testosterone should be checked for totals between 230 and 350 ng/dL.

paras: It is a blood draw, ideally in the morning, ordered through a doctor or a direct-to-consumer lab. People often repeat it after lifestyle or treatment changes to compare results over time.

The test itself is a routine blood draw. The caveats are interpretive: levels vary through the day, assays differ, free testosterone can be estimated or measured by equilibrium dialysis or mass spectrometry, and the free androgen index is considered a poor predictor of it. Interpretation belongs with a clinician.

angle.text: This panel shows where your testosterone, SHBG, estradiol and LH stand, so hormone-focused steps toward muscle, leanness and skin start from real numbers. The tests are standard tools for diagnosing low testosterone.

lead: A hormone bloodwork panel typically measures total testosterone, free or bioavailable testosterone, sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), estradiol (E2) and luteinizing hormone (LH). People use it to see what their hormones are actually doing before and while working on their physique, skin and hair, since these hormones influence muscle growth, body fat, oil production, hair growth and recovery [1][2].

Testosterone promotes muscle mass and strength, drives beard and body hair, enlarges sebaceous glands (which can mean oilier skin and acne), and is linked to male pattern hair loss in people who are genetically predisposed [2]. Estradiol and SHBG shape how much of that testosterone is available: only about 1 to 4 percent of circulating testosterone and estradiol is free, and a higher SHBG means less free hormone [3][2]. The panel gives people numbers to connect with how they look and feel.

Clinically, the panel is how low testosterone is identified, with LH checked to find the cause [1]. Endocrine Society guidance recommends diagnosing hypogonadism only in men with symptoms and consistently low testosterone, using a fasting morning total testosterone measurement as the first test [4].
infobox: Total T, free T, SHBG, E2, LH
Fasting morning draw recommended for the first test [4]
About 240 to 950 ng/dL, falling roughly 1 to 3 percent a year [1]

paras: Total testosterone is the amount in blood including protein-bound hormone. Most testosterone is bound to albumin or SHBG, and only a small free fraction is considered biologically active [2][3]. SHBG is a liver-made protein that binds androgens and estrogens; Wikipedia lists estrogen-rich states, hyperthyroidism and cirrhosis as raising it, and obesity, insulin resistance, hypothyroidism and androgens as lowering it [3].

LH is the pituitary signal that tells the testes to make testosterone. Primary hypogonadism usually shows elevated LH or FSH, while secondary hypogonadism shows normal or low levels [1]. Estradiol is measured because fat tissue converts testosterone to estradiol through aromatase [2].

Guidelines cited by Wikipedia say a total testosterone below 300 ng/dL can support a diagnosis, treatment is often prescribed below 230 ng/dL with symptoms, and free or bioavailable testosterone should be checked for totals between 230 and 350 ng/dL [1]. Normal total testosterone generally ranges from about 240 to 950 ng/dL, and testosterone can drop up to 13 percent over the day, so reference ranges are based on morning samples [1].

An Endocrine Society position statement expressed dissatisfaction with most testosterone assays. Accurate free testosterone generally needs equilibrium dialysis or mass spectrometry, and the free androgen index is described as the worst predictor [1]. A 2019 review notes that measuring free testosterone is endorsed by recent clinical practice guidelines but remains debated, that assays are not harmonized, and that calculated free T equations are imperfect but can still give clinically useful results. It also says the free androgen index is not recommended in men because of inaccuracy at extremes of SHBG [5]. As of 2018 screening men without symptoms is not recommended [1].

Panels are a frequent topic on T Nation, where members compare free testosterone results, discuss unusual SHBG values and share bloodwork [6][7]. In one thread a member shared a family member's panel with high SHBG and low free testosterone and asked about options [7]. The threads mix personal results with opinion and are not clinical guidance.

No studies found on the panel as a looksmaxxing practice. The Endocrine Society's 2018 guideline sets out how testosterone deficiency should be diagnosed with symptoms and repeated morning measurements [4]. A 2019 review summarises how free testosterone is assessed and the limits of each method [5]. A case report describes a man whose declining performance and low libido led to testosterone testing and eventual diagnosis of a nonfunctioning pituitary macroadenoma, illustrating the panel's diagnostic use [8].

lore.intro: On T Nation, members post hormone panels, ask what their numbers mean and compare free testosterone and SHBG values [6][7].
